entries.4a9c6f50e87bc1e970ce18672f77566146ccb121: <div sID="gen20997" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Zech.13" sID="Zech.13"/> <div eID="gen20997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20998" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20999" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Some further promises relating to gospel-times. Here is a promise of the remission of sins (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">ver. 1</reference>), of the reformation of manners (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.2">ver. 2</reference>), and particularly of the convicting and silencing of false prophets, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.2-Zech.13.6">ver. 2-6</reference>. II. A clear prediction of the sufferings of Christ and the dispersion of his disciples thereupon (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">ver. 7</reference>), of the destruction of the greater part of the Jewish nation not long after (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">ver. 8</reference>), and of the purifying of a remnant of them, a peculiar people to God, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">ver. 9</reference>.
entries.40c6afa2a8b53a56da850bd1b2df896b8bea64fe: <div eID="gen20999" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20998" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Predictions; The Destruction of False Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 500.)</title> <div sID="gen21000" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they shall no more be remembered: and also I will cause the prophets and the unclean spirit to pass out of the land. <hi type="super">3</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when any shall yet prophesy, then his father and his mother that begat him shall say unto him, Thou shalt not live; for thou speakest lies in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and his father and his mother that begat him shall thrust him through when he prophesieth. <hi type="super">4</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the prophets shall be ashamed every one of his vision, when he hath prophesied; neither shall they wear a rough garment to deceive: <hi type="super">5</hi> But he shall say, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> no prophet, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a husbandman; for man taught me to keep cattle from my youth. <hi type="super">6</hi> And <hi type="italic">one</hi> shall say unto him, What <hi type="italic">are</hi> these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, <hi type="italic">Those</hi> with which I was wounded <hi type="italic">in</hi> the house of my friends. <div eID="gen21000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21001" type="x-p"/> Behold the Lamb of God <hi type="italic">taking away the sin of the world,</hi> the sin of the church; for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> was the Son of God manifested, to <hi type="italic">take away our sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.5">1 John iii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen21001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21002" type="x-p"/> I. He takes away the guilt of sin by the blood of his cross (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day,</hi> in the gospel-day, <hi type="italic">there shall be a fountain opened,</hi> that is, provision made for the cleansing of all those from the pollutions of sin who truly repent and are sorry for them. <hi type="italic">In that day,</hi> when the Spirit of grace is poured out to set them a mourning for their sins, they shall not mourn as those who have no hope, but they shall have their sins pardoned, and the comfort of their pardon in their bosoms. Their consciences shall be purified and pacified by the <hi type="italic">blood of Christ, which cleanses from all sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.1.7">1 John i. 7</reference>. For Christ is exalted to give both repentance and remission of sins; and where he gives the one no doubt he gives the other. This <hi type="italic">fountain opened</hi> is the pierced side of Jesus Christ, spoken of just before (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">ch. xii. 10</reference>), for thence came there out <hi type="italic">blood and water,</hi> and both for cleansing. And those who <hi type="italic">look upon Christ pierced,</hi> and mourn for their sins that pierced him, and are therefore in bitterness for him, may look again upon Christ pierced and rejoice in him, because it pleased the Lord thus to smite this rock, that it might be to us a <hi type="italic">fountain of living waters.</hi> See here, 1. How we are polluted; we are all so; we have sinned, and sin is uncleanness; it defiles the mind and conscience, renders us odious to God and uneasy in ourselves, unfit to be employed in the service of God and admitted into communion with him, as those who were ceremonially unclean were shut out of the sanctuary. The <hi type="italic">house of David</hi> and the <hi type="italic">inhabitants of Jerusalem</hi> are under <hi type="italic">sin,</hi> which is uncleanness. The truth is, we are all <hi type="italic">as an unclean thing,</hi> and deserve to have our portion with the unclean. 2. How we may be purged. Behold, there is fountain opened for us to wash in, and there are streams flowing to us from that fountain, so that, if we be not made clean, it is our own fault. The blood of Christ, and God's pardoning mercy in that blood, revealed in the new covenant, are, (1.) A fountain; for there is in them an inexhaustible fulness. There is mercy enough in God, and merit enough in Christ, for the forgiving of the greatest sins and sinners, upon gospel-terms. <hi type="italic">Such were some of you, but you are washed,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>. Under the law there were a brazen laver and a brazen sea to wash in; those were but vessels, but we have a fountain to ourselves, overflowing, ever-flowing. (2.) <hi type="italic">A fountain opened;</hi> for, whoever will, may come and take the benefit of it; it is opened, not only to <hi type="italic">the house of David,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">the inhabitants of Jerusalem,</hi> to the poor and mean as well as to the rich and great; or it is opened for all believers, who, as the spiritual seed of Christ, are of the house of David, and, as living members of the church, are inhabitants of Jerusalem. Through Christ all that believe are justified, are <hi type="italic">washed from their sins in his blood,</hi> that they may be <hi type="italic">made to our God kings and priests,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5-Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen21002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21003" type="x-p"/> II. He takes away the dominion of sin by the power of his grace, even of beloved sins. This evermore accompanies the former; those that are washed in the fountain opened, as they are justified, so they are sanctified; the water came with the blood out of the pierced side of Christ. It is here promised that in that day, 1. Idolatry shall be quite abolished and the people of the Jews shall be effectually cured of their inclination to it (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land.</hi> The worship of the idols of their fathers shall be so perfectly rooted out that in one generation or two it shall be forgotten that ever there were such idols among them; they shall either not be named at all or not with any respect; <hi type="italic">they shall no more be remembered,</hi> as was promised, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.17">Hos. ii. 17</reference>. This was fulfilled in the rooted aversion which the Jews had, after the captivity, to idols and idolatry, and still retain to this day; it was fulfilled also in the ready conversion of many to the faith of Christ, by which they were taken off from making an idol of the ceremonial law, as the unbelieving Jews did; and it is still in the fulfilling when souls are brought off from the world and the flesh, those two great idols, that they may cleave to God only. 2. False prophecy shall also be brought to an end: <hi type="italic">I will cause the prophets and the unclean spirit,</hi> the prophets that are under the influence of the unclean spirit, to <hi type="italic">pass out of the land.</hi> The devil is an <hi type="italic">unclean</hi> spirit; sin and uncleanness are from him; he has his prophets, that serve his interests and receive their instructions from him. Take away the unclean spirit, and the prophets would not deceive as they do; take away the false prophets that produce sham commissions, and the unclean spirit could not do the mischief he does. When God designs the silencing of the false prophets he banishes the unclean spirit out of the land, that wrought in them, and was a rival with him for the throne in the heart. The church of the Jews, when they were addicted to idols, did also dote much upon false prophets, who flattered them in their sins with promises of impunity and peace; but here it is promised, as a blessed effect of the promised reformation, that they should be very much set against false prophets, and zealous to clear the land of them; they were so after the captivity, till, through the blindness of their zeal against false prophets, they had put Christ to death under that character, and, after that, there arose many <hi type="italic">false Christs and false prophets, and deceived many,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.11">Matt. xxiv. 11</reference>. It is here foretold, (1.) That false prophets, instead of being indulged and favoured, should be brought to condign punishment even by their nearest relations, which would be as great an instance as any of flagrant zeal against those deceivers (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">When any shall</hi> set up for a prophet, and shall <hi type="italic">speak lies in the name of the Lord,</hi> shall preach that which tends to draw people from God and to confirm them in sin, his own parents shall be the first and most forward to prosecute him for it, according to the law. <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6-Deut.13.11">Deut. xiii. 6-11</reference>, "<hi type="italic">If thy son entice thee secretly</hi> from God, <hi type="italic">thou shalt surely kill him.</hi> Show thy indignation against him, and prevent any further temptation from him." His <hi type="italic">father and his mother shall thrust him through when he prophesies.</hi> Note, We ought to conceive, and always to retain, a very great detestation and dread of every thing that would draw us out of the way of our duty into by-paths, as those who cannot <hi type="italic">bear that which is evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.22">Rev. ii. 2</reference>. And holy zeal for God and godliness will make us hate sin, and dread temptation, most in those whom naturally we love best, and who are nearest to us; there our danger is greatest, as Adam's from Eve, Job's from his wife; and there it will be the most praiseworthy to show our zeal, as Levi, who, in the cause of God, did not <hi type="italic">acknowledge his brethren,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">know his own children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. Thus we must hate and forsake our nearest relations when they come in competition with our duty to God, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Luke xiv. 26</reference>. Natural affections, even the strongest, must be over-ruled by gracious affections. (2.) That false prophets should be themselves convinced of their sin and folly, and let fall their pretensions (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The prophets shall be ashamed every one of his vision;</hi> they shall not repeat it, or insist upon it, but desire that it may be forgotten and no more said of it, being ready themselves to own it was a sham, because God has by his grace awakened their consciences and shown them their error, or because the event disproves their predictions, and gives them the lie, or because their prophecies do not meet with such a favourable reception as they used to meet with, but are generally despised and distasted; they perceive the people ashamed of them, which makes them begin to be ashamed of themselves. And therefore they shall no longer <hi type="italic">wear a rough garment,</hi> or <hi type="italic">garment of hair,</hi> as the true prophets used to do, in imitation of Elijah, and in token of their being mortified to the pleasures and delights of sense." The pretenders had appeared in the habit of true prophets; but, their folly being now made manifest, they shall lay it aside, no more to deceive and impose upon unthinking unwary people by it. A modest dress is a very good thing, if it be the genuine indication of a humble heart, and is to instruct; but it is a bad thing if it be the hypocritical disguise of a proud ambitious heart, and is to deceive. Let men be really as good as they seem to be, but not seem to be better than really they are. This pretender, as a true penitent, [1.] Shall undeceive those whom he had imposed upon: <hi type="italic">He shall say, "I am no prophet,</hi> as I have pretended to be, was never designed nor set apart to the office, never educated nor brought up for it, never conversant among the sons of the prophets. <hi type="italic">I am a husbandman,</hi> and was bred to that business; I was never taught of God to prophesy, but <hi type="italic">taught of man to keep cattle</hi>" Amos was originally such a one too, and yet was afterwards called to be a prophet, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.14-Amos.7.15">Amos vii. 14, 15</reference>. But this deceiver never had any such call. Note, Those who sorrow after a godly sort for their having deceived others will be forward to confess their sin, and will be so just as to rectify the mistakes which they have been the cause of. Thus those who had <hi type="italic">used curious arts,</hi> when they were converted <hi type="italic">showed their deeds,</hi> and by what fallacies they had cheated the people, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.18">Acts xix. 18</reference>. [2.] He shall return to his own proper employment, which is the fittest for him: <hi type="italic">I will be a husbandman</hi> (so it may be read); "I will apply myself to my calling again, and meddle no more with things that belong not to me; for <hi type="italic">man taught me to keep cattle from my youth,</hi> and cattle I will again keep, and never set up for a preacher any more." Note, When we are convinced that we have gone out of the way of our duty we must evince the truth of our repentance by returning to it again, though it be the severest mortification to us. [3.] He shall acknowledge those to be his friends who by a severe discipline were instrumental to bring him to a sight of his error, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.6">v. 6</reference>. When he who with the greatest assurance had asserted himself so lately to be a prophet suddenly drops his claims, and says, I am no prophet, every body will be surprised at it, and some will ask, "<hi type="italic">What are these wounds,</hi> or marks of stripes, <hi type="italic">in thy hands?</hi> how camest thou by them? Hast thou not been <hi type="italic">examined by scourging?</hi> And is not that it that has brought thee to thyself?" (<hi type="italic">Vexatio dat intellectum—Vexation sharpens the intellect.</hi>) "Hast thou not been beaten into this acknowledgment? Was it not the rod and reproof that gave thee this wisdom?" And he shall own, "Yes, it was; these are the <hi type="italic">wounds with which I was wounded in the house of my friends,</hi> who bound me, and used me hardly and severely, as a distracted man, and so brought me to my senses." By this it appears that those parents of the false prophet that <hi type="italic">thrust him through</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.3">v. 3</reference>) did not do it till they had first tried to reclaim him by correction, and he would not be reclaimed; for so was the law concerning a disobedient son—his parents must first have chastened him in vain before they were allowed to bring him forth to be stoned, <reference osisRef="Deut.21.18-Deut.21.19">Deut. xxi. 18, 19</reference>. But here is another who was reduced by stripes, and so prevented the capital punishment; and he had the sense and honesty to own that they were his friends, his real friends, who thus wounded him, that they might reclaim him; for <hi type="italic">faithful are the wounds of a friend,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.6">Prov. xxvii. 6</reference>. Some good interpreters, observing how soon this comes after the mention of Christ's being pierced, think that these are the words of that great prophet, not of the false prophet spoken of before. Christ was wounded in his hands, when they were nailed to the cross, and, after his resurrection, he had the marks of these wounds; and here he tells how he came by them; he received them as a false prophet, for the chief priests called him a deceiver, and upon that account would have him crucified; but he received them in the house of his friends—the Jews, who should have been his friends; for <hi type="italic">he came to his own,</hi> and, though they were his bitter enemies, yet he was pleased to call them his <hi type="italic">friends,</hi> as he did Judas (<hi type="italic">Friend, wherefore hast thou come?</hi>) because they forwarded his sufferings for him; as he called Peter <hi type="italic">Satan—an adversary,</hi> because he dissuaded him from them.
entries.666cc0149b6a0d6c2d4cb1f1c554f1ff58df3d5f: <div eID="gen21003" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sufferings of Christ Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 500.)</title> <div sID="gen21004" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man <hi type="italic">that is</hi> my fellow, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones. <hi type="super">8</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> in all the land, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , two parts therein shall be cut off <hi type="italic">and</hi> die; but the third shall be left therein. <hi type="super">9</hi> And I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them: I will say, It <hi type="italic">is</hi> my people: and they shall say, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> my God. <div eID="gen21004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21005" type="x-p"/> Here is a prophecy, <div eID="gen21005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21006" type="x-p"/> I. Of the sufferings of Christ, of him who was to be pierced, and was to be the fountain opened. <hi type="italic">Awake, O sword! against my Shepherd,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">v. 7</reference>. These are the words of God the Father, giving order and commission to the sword of his justice to awake against his Son, when he had voluntarily made his soul an offering for sin; for <hi type="italic">it pleased the Lord to bruise him</hi> and <hi type="italic">put him to grief;</hi> and <hi type="italic">he was stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Isa. liii. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">10</reference>. Observe, 1. How he calls him. "As God, he is <hi type="italic">my fellow;</hi>" for he thought it <hi type="italic">no robbery to be equal with God.</hi> He and <hi type="italic">the Father</hi> are <hi type="italic">one.</hi> He was from eternity by him, as one brought up with him, and, in the work of man's redemption, he was his elect, in whom his soul delighted, and the counsel of peace was between them both. "As Mediator, he is <hi type="italic">my Shepherd,</hi> that great and good Shepherd that undertook to feed the flock," <reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">ch. xi. 7</reference>. He is the Shepherd that was to lay down his life for the sheep. 2. How he uses him: <hi type="italic">Awake, O sword! against him.</hi> If he will be a sacrifice, he must be slain, for without the shedding of blood, the life-blood, there was no remission. Men thrust him through as the good Shepherd (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.13.3">v. 3</reference>), that he might <hi type="italic">purchase the flock of God</hi> with <hi type="italic">his own blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Acts xx. 28</reference>. It is not a charge given to a rod to correct him, but to a sword to slay him; for <hi type="italic">Messiah the prince must be cut off, but not for himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>. It is not the sword of war that receives this charge, that he may die in the bed of honour, but the sword of justice, that he may die as a criminal, upon an ignominious tree. This sword must awake against him; he having no sin of his own to answer for, the sword of justice had nothing to say to him of itself, till, by particular order from the Judge of all, it was warranted to brandish itself against him. He was the Lamb <hi type="italic">slain from the foundation of the world,</hi> in the decree and counsel of God; but the sword designed against him had long slumbered, till now at length it is called upon to awake, not, "Awake, and smite him; strike home; not with a drowsy blow, but an awakened one;" for God <hi type="italic">spared not his own Son.</hi> <div eID="gen21006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21007" type="x-p"/> II. Of the dispersion of the disciples thereupon: <hi type="italic">Smite the Shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.</hi> This our Lord Jesus himself declares to have been fulfilled when <hi type="italic">all his disciples were offended because of him</hi> in the night wherein he was betrayed, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.31">Matt. xxvi. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.27">Mark xiv. 27</reference>. They all <hi type="italic">forsook him and fled.</hi> The smiting of the Shepherd is the scattering of the sheep. They were <hi type="italic">scattered every one to his own, and left him alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.32">John xvi. 32</reference>. Herein they were like timorous sheep; yet the Shepherd thus provided for their safety, for he said, <hi type="italic">If you seek me, let these go their way.</hi> Some make another application of this; Christ was the <hi type="italic">Shepherd</hi> of the Jewish nation; he was smitten; they themselves smote him, and therefore they were justly scattered abroad, and dispersed among the nations, and remain so at this day. These words, <hi type="italic">I will turn my hand upon the little ones,</hi> may be understood either as a threatening (as Christ suffered, so shall his disciples, they shall <hi type="italic">drink of the cup that he drank of</hi> and be <hi type="italic">baptized with the baptism that he was baptized</hi> with) or as a promise that God would gather Christ's scattered disciples together again, and he should give them the meeting in Galilee. Though the little ones among Christ's soldiers may be dispersed, they shall rally again; the lambs of his flock, though frightened by the beasts of prey, shall recover themselves, shall be gathered in his arms and laid in his bosom. Sometimes, when the sheep are scattered and lost in the wilderness, yet the little ones, which, it was feared, would be a prey (<reference osisRef="Num.14.31">Num. xiv. 31</reference>), are brought in, are brought home, and God turns his hand upon them. <div eID="gen21007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21008" type="x-p"/> III. Of the rejection and ruin of the unbelieving Jews (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">v. 8</reference>); and this word has, and shall have, its accomplishment, in the destruction of the corrupt and hypocritical part of the church. <hi type="italic">It shall come to pass that in all the land of Israel two parts shall be cut off and die.</hi> The Roman army laid the country waste, and slew at least two-thirds of the Jews. Some understand by the <hi type="italic">cutting off,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dying,</hi> or <hi type="italic">two parts</hi> in all <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> the abolishing of heathenism and Judaism, that Christianity, the third part, might be left to reign alone. The Jewish worship was quite taken away by the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple. And, some time after, Pagan idolatry was in a manner extirpated, when the empire became Christian. <div eID="gen21008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21009" type="x-p"/> IV. Of the reformation and preservation of the chosen remnant, those of them that believed, and the Christian church in general (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The third part shall be left.</hi> When Jerusalem and Judea were destroyed, all the Christians in that country, having among them the warning Christ gave them to <hi type="italic">flee to the mountains,</hi> shifted for their own safety, and were sheltered in a city called <hi type="italic">Pella,</hi> on the other side Jordan. We have here first the trials and then the triumphs of the Christian church, and of all the faithful members of it. 1. Their trials: <hi type="italic">I will bring</hi> that <hi type="italic">third part through the fire</hi> of affliction. <hi type="italic">and will refine</hi> and <hi type="italic">try them</hi> as <hi type="italic">silver and gold are refined and tried.</hi> This was fulfilled in the persecutions of the primitive church, the <hi type="italic">fiery trial</hi> which tried the people of God then, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.12">1 Pet. iv. 12</reference>. Those whom God sets apart for himself must pass through a probation and purification in this world; they must be <hi type="italic">tried</hi> that <hi type="italic">their faith</hi> may be <hi type="italic">found to praise and honour</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6-1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. i. 6, 7</reference>), as Abraham's faith was when it was tried by the command given him to offer up Isaac, <hi type="italic">Now know I that thou fearest me.</hi> They must be tried, that both those that are perfect and those that are not may be <hi type="italic">made manifest.</hi> They must be refined from their dross; their corruption must be purged out; they must be brightened and bettered. 2. Their triumphs. (1.) Their communion with God is their triumph: <hi type="italic">They shall call on my name, and I will hear them.</hi> They write to God by prayer, and receive from him answers of peace, and thus keep up a comfortable communion with him. <hi type="italic">This honour have all his saints.</hi> (2.) Their covenant with God is their triumph: "<hi type="italic">I will say, It is my people,</hi> whom I have chosen and loved, and will own; <hi type="italic">and they shall say, the Lord is my God,</hi> and a God all-sufficient to me; and in me they shall boast every day and all the day long. <hi type="italic">This God is our God for ever and ever.</hi>"  <chapter eID="Zech.13"/> <div eID="gen21009" type="x-p"/>

entries.a3ea9428e2c5998b300f97218f176471f6f88338: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13183"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.13.1-Zech.13.9">Zec 13:1-9</reference>. Cleansing of the Jews from Sin; Abolition of Idolatry; the Shepherd Smitten; the People of the Land Cut Off, except a Third Part Refined by Trials.</title> <div sID="gen24877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13183"/>1. Connected with the close of the twelfth chapter. The mourning penitents are here comforted.<div eID="gen24877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fountain opened--</hi>It has been long opened, but then first it shall be so "to the house of David," &c. (representing all Israel) after their long and weary wanderings. Like Hagar in the wilderness they remain ignorant of the refreshment near them, until God "opens their eyes" (<reference osisRef="Gen.21.19">Ge 21:19</reference>) [Moore]. It is not the fountain, but their eyes that need to be opened. It shall be a "fountain" ever flowing; not a laver needing constantly to be replenished with water, such as stood between the tabernacle and altar (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.18">Ex 30:18</reference>).<div eID="gen24878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for sin ... uncleanness--</hi>that is, judicial guilt and moral impurity. Thus justification and sanctification are implied in this verse as both flowing from the blood of Christ, not from ceremonial sacrifices (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">He 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.7">1Jo 1:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25">Eze 36:25</reference>). Sin in Hebrew is literally a missing the mark or way. <div eID="gen24879" type="x-p"/>
entries.96b647071897df09d9e188ad9e078ef23f873233: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13184"/><div sID="gen24880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13184"/>2. Consequences of pardon; not indolence, but the extirpation of sin.<div eID="gen24880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">names of ... idols--</hi>Their very names were not to be mentioned; thus the Jews, instead of Mephibaal, said Mephibosheth (Bosheth meaning a contemptible thing) (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.13">Ex 23:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.3">De 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.4">Psa 16:4</reference>).<div eID="gen24881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of the land--</hi>Judea's two great sins, idolatry and false prophecy, have long since ceased. But these are types of all sin (for example, covetousness, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>, a besetting sin of the Jews now). Idolatry, combined with the "spirit" of "Satan," is again to be incarnated in "the man of sin," who is to arise in Judea (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3-2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:3-12</reference>), and is to be "consumed with the Spirit of the Lord's mouth." Compare as to Antichrist's papal precursor, "seducing spirits ... doctrines of devils," &c., <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1">2Pe 2:1</reference>.<div eID="gen24882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the unclean spirit--</hi>Hebrew, spirit of uncleanness (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.16.13">Re 16:13</reference>); opposed to "the Spirit of holiness" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>), "spirit of error" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.6">1Jo 4:6</reference>). One assuming to be divinely inspired, but in league with Satan. <div eID="gen24883" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bd52c68ec757e2c882595d777b38ded9c1d211b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13185"/><div sID="gen24884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13185"/>3. The form of phraseology here is drawn from <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6-Deut.10.18">De 13:6-10; 18</reference>:<reference osisRef="Deut.10.20">20</reference>. The substantial truth expressed is that false prophecy shall be utterly abolished. If it were possible for it again to start up, the very parents of the false prophet would not let parental affection interfere, but would be the first to thrust him through. Love to Christ must be paramount to the tenderest of natural ties (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.37">Mt 10:37</reference>). Much as the godly love their children, they love God and His honor more. <div eID="gen24884" type="x-p"/>
entries.f04bf36a3725e3db6661555b141129b724e8cb72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13186"/><div sID="gen24885" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13186"/><hi type="bold">4. prophets ... ashamed--</hi>of the false prophecies which they have uttered in times past, and which the event has confuted.<div eID="gen24885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rough garment--</hi>sackcloth. The badge of a prophet (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.8">2Ki 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.2">Is 20:2</reference>), to mark their frugality alike in food and attire (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.4">Mt 3:4</reference>); also, to be consonant to the mournful warnings which they delivered. It is not the dress that is here condemned, but the purpose for which it was worn, namely, to conceal wolves under sheep's clothing [Calvin]. The monkish hair-shirt of Popery, worn to inspire the multitude with the impression of superior sanctity, shall be then cast aside. <div eID="gen24886" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c0e7be800b5ef63b5edf756036b9870eeddb6ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13187"/><div sID="gen24887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13187"/>5-6. The detection of one of the false prophets dramatically represented. He is seized by some zealous vindicator of the law, and in fear cries out, "I am no prophet."<div eID="gen24887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">man--</hi>that is, one.<div eID="gen24888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taught me to keep cattle--</hi>As "keeping cattle" is not the same as to be "an husbandman," translate rather, "Has used (or 'appropriated') me as a servant," namely, in husbandry [Maurer]. However, husbandry and keeping cattle might be regarded as jointly the occupation of the person questioned: then <reference osisRef="Amos.7.14">Am 7:14</reference>, "herdman," will accord with English Version. A Hebrew kindred word means "cattle." Both occupations, the respondent replies, are inconsistent with my being a "prophet." <div eID="gen24889" type="x-p"/>
entries.b16da871511ff9ef100750bb5a14fc108a13cc27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13189"/><div sID="gen24892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13189"/>7. Expounded by Christ as referring to Himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.31">Mt 26:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.32">32</reference>). Thus it is a resumption of the prophecy of His betrayal (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.4">Zec 11:4</reference>, 10, 13, 14), and the subsequent punishment of the Jews. It explains the mystery why He, who came to be a blessing, was cut off while bestowing the blessing. God regards sin in such a fearful light that He spared not His own co-equal Son in the one Godhead, when that Son bore the sinner's guilt.<div eID="gen24892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Awake--</hi>Compare a similar address to the sword of justice personified (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.6">Jr 46:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.7">7</reference>). For "smite" (imperative), <reference osisRef="Matt.26.31">Mt 26:31</reference> has "I will smite." The act of the sword, it is thus implied, is God's act. So the prophecy in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>, "Hear ye," is imperative; the fulfilment as declared by Jesus is future (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.14">Mt 13:14</reference>), "ye shall hear."<div eID="gen24893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword--</hi>the symbol of judicial power, the highest exercise of which is to take away the life of the condemned (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Psa 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Ro 13:4</reference>). Not merely a show, or expression, of justice (as Socinians think) is distinctly implied here, but an actual execution of it on Messiah the shepherd, the substitute for the sheep, by God as judge. Yet God in this shows His love as gloriously as His justice. For God calls Messiah "My shepherd," that is, provided (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Re 13:8</reference>) for sinners by My love to them, and ever the object of My love, though judicially smitten (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Is 53:4</reference>) for their sins (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">59:16</reference>).<div eID="gen24894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">man that is my fellow--</hi>literally, "the man of my union." The Hebrew for "man" is "a mighty man," one peculiarly man in his noblest ideal. "My fellow," that is, "my associate." "My equal" ([De Wette]; a remarkable admission from a Rationalist). "My nearest kinsman" [Hengstenberg], (<reference osisRef="John.10.30">Joh 10:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.10">14:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.6">Php 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen24895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sheep shall be scattered--</hi>The scattering of Christ's disciples on His apprehension was the partial fulfilment (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.31">Mt 26:31</reference>), a pledge of the dispersion of the Jewish nation (once the Lord's sheep, <reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>) consequent on their crucifixion of Him. The Jews, though "scattered," are still the Lord's "sheep," awaiting their being "gathered" by Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.9">Is 40:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen24896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will turn ... hand upon ... little ones--</hi>that is, I will interpose in favor of (compare the phrase in a good sense, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Is 1:25</reference>) "the little ones," namely, the humble followers of Christ from the Jewish Church, despised by the world: "the poor of the flock" (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">Zec 11:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.11">11</reference>); comforted after His crucifixion at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="John.20.17-John.20.20">Joh 20:17-20</reference>); saved again by a special interposition from the destruction of Jerusalem, having retired to Pella when Cestius Gallus so unaccountably withdrew from Jerusalem. Ever since there has been a Jewish "remnant" of "the little ones ... according to the election of grace." The hand of Jehovah was laid in wrath on the Shepherd that His hand might be turned in grace upon the little ones. <div eID="gen24897" type="x-p"/>
entries.c490599d7e0b51a1be4690d946f672307bef1a33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13190"/><div sID="gen24898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13190"/>8-9. Two-thirds of the Jewish nation were to perish in the Roman wars, and a third to survive. Probably from the context (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.2-Zech.14.9">Zec 14:2-9</reference>), which has never yet been fulfilled, the destruction of the two-thirds (literally, "the proportion of two," or "portion of two") and the saving of the remnant, the one-third, are still future, and to be fulfilled under Antichrist. <div eID="gen24898" type="x-p"/>

entries.40994529e7f4aff2918883b86bf6632a8b3a4652: <div eID="gen35747" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35748" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35749" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35749" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35748" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35750" type="x-p"/> After the humiliation and conversion of the Jews, foretold in the preceding chapter, they are here promised the full pardon of their sins, and a deliverance from idolatry and false prophets, <reference osisRef="Zac.13.1-Zac.13.6">Zac 13:1-6</reference>. Prophecy concerning the death of the Messiah, and the persecution of his disciples, <reference osisRef="Zac.13.7">Zac 13:7</reference>. The remaining verses may refer to those Jewish converts to Christianity who survived the calamities which their country suffered from the Romans, <reference osisRef="Zac.13.8">Zac 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zac.13.9">Zac 13:9</reference>. <div eID="gen35750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35751" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35752" type="x-p"/> In that day there shall be a fountain opened - This chapter is a continuation of the preceding, and should not have been separated from it. <div eID="gen35752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35753" type="x-p"/> A fountain - The source of mercy in Christ Jesus; perhaps referring to the death he should die, and the piercing of his side, when blood and water issued out. <div eID="gen35753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35754" type="x-p"/> To the house of David - To David's family, and such like persons as it included. See the history of David and his sons, and then learn for whom Christ shed his blood. <div eID="gen35754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35755" type="x-p"/> Inhabitants of Jerusalem - Such like persons as the Jews were in every part of their history, and in their last times, when they clamoured for the blood of Christ, and pursued him unto death! Learn from this also for whom Christ died! These were the worst of the human race; and if he died for them, none need despair. They rejected, betrayed, crucified, slew, and blasphemed Christ, and afterwards persecuted his followers. For these he died! Yes: and he tasted death for Every Man. <div eID="gen35755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35756" type="x-p"/> For sin and for uncleanness - For the removal of the guilt of sin, and for the purification of the soul from the uncleanness or pollution of sin.
entries.a27cef2a5b90e86eccdc2cf95f0556f211faaa0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35757" type="x-p"/> I will cut off the names of the idols - There shall not only be no idolatry, but the very names of the idols shall be forgotten, or be held in such abhorrence that no person shall mention them. This prophecy seems to be ancient, and to have been delivered while idolatry had prevalence in Israel and Judah. <div eID="gen35757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35758" type="x-p"/> I will cause the prophets - All false teachers. <div eID="gen35758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35759" type="x-p"/> And the unclean spirit - That which leads to impurity, the spirit of divination; the lust of the flesh, and of the eye, and the pride of life. Satan shall have neither a being in, nor power over, the hearts of sincere believers in Christ.
entries.8d26ded15ea490fb734279d464c6ab30cc34117a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35760" type="x-p"/> When any shall yet prophesy - Falsely; such shall be the horror of such an evil, that there shall be no toleration of it. Itself, and they who practice it, shall be everywhere destroyed.
entries.8238c71b55b88eac51613239360d11a304275264: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35761" type="x-p"/> Neither shall they wear a rough garment - A rough garment made of goats' hair, coarse wool, or the course pile of the camel, was the ordinary garb of God's prophets. And the false prophets wore the same; for they pretended to the same gifts, and the same spirit, and therefore they wore the same kind of garments. John Baptist had a garment of this kind.
entries.3a5f49fa60c5c1d9d7ec94246ce33318ee1e2348: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35762" type="x-p"/> But he shall say, I am no prophet - This must be the case of a false prophet or diviner, who had been obliged to give up his infamous practice, and become even a laborer in the land. But having been known to be such, he is questioned by the people to see if he still were addicted in heart to the same practices. He declares he is no prophet, neither true nor false; that he is now a husbandman, and was brought up a herdsman.
entries.b2dd68e9c4b12a866ee235c4cd0e55d0bccbe467: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35763" type="x-p"/> What are these wounds in thine hands? - Marks which he had received in honor of his idols. But he shall excuse himself by stating that he had received these marks in his own family; when, most probably, they had been dedicated to some of those idols. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa 44:5</reference>. I do not think that these words are spoken at all concerning Jesus Christ. I have heard them quoted in this way; but I cannot hear such an application of them without horror. In quoting from the Old Testament in reference to the New, we cannot be too cautious. We may wound the truth instead of honoring it.
entries.47050dcc5312ee058d5c1a88b8701d36892ffa2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35764" type="x-p"/> Awake, O sword, against my Shepherd - This is generally understood of Jesus Christ. The sword is that of Divine justice which seemed to have been long asleep, and should long ago have struck either Man, or his Substitute, the Messiah. Jesus is here called God's Shepherd, because he had appointed him to feed and govern, as well as to save, the whole lost world. This is a prosopopoeia, and the address to the sword is very poetic. There is a fine passage in Aeschylus to the same effect: - Ξενος δε κληροις επινωμᾳ, Χαλυβος Σκυθων αποικας, Κτεανων χρηματοδαιτας Πικρος, ωμοφρων σιδαρος, Χθονα ναιειν διαπηλας Ὁποσαν αν και φθιμενοισι κατεχειν, Των μεγαλων πεδιων αμοιροις, <div eID="gen35764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35765" type="x-p"/> Aeschyl. Sept. cont. Hebrews 733. "The rude barbarian, from the mines <div eID="gen35765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35766" type="x-p"/> Of Scythia, o'er the lots presides; <div eID="gen35766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35767" type="x-p"/> Ruthless to each his share assigns, <div eID="gen35767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35768" type="x-p"/> And the contested realm divides: <div eID="gen35768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35769" type="x-p"/> To each allots no wider a domain <div eID="gen35769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35770" type="x-p"/> Than, on the cold earth as they lie, <div eID="gen35770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35771" type="x-p"/> Their breathless bodies occupy, <div eID="gen35771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35772" type="x-p"/> Regardless of an ampler reign: <div eID="gen35772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35773" type="x-p"/> Such narrow compass does the sword - <div eID="gen35773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35774" type="x-p"/> A cruel umpire - their high claims afford." <div eID="gen35774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35775" type="x-p"/> Potter. <div eID="gen35775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35776" type="x-p"/> The man that is my Fellow - ועל גבר עמיתי veal geber amithi, "upon the strong man," or "the hero that is with Me;" my neighbor. "The Word was God, and the Word was With God;" <reference osisRef="Joh.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>. "I and my Father are One;" <reference osisRef="Joh.10.30">Joh 10:30</reference>. <div eID="gen35776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35777" type="x-p"/> Smite the Shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered - This is quoted by our Lord, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.31">Mat 26:31</reference>, in relation to his disciples, who should be scattered on his crucifixion: and they were so; for every one, giving up all for lost, went to his own house. <div eID="gen35777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35778" type="x-p"/> And I will turn mine hand upon the little ones - I will take care of the little flock, and preserve them from Jewish malice and Gentile persecution. And so this little flock was most wondrously preserved, and has been increasing from year to year from that time to the present day.
entries.bc52963297a2bfe5854ee8c325a60b2ee86704d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35779" type="x-p"/> Two parts therein shall be cut off - In the war with the Romans. <div eID="gen35779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35780" type="x-p"/> But the third shall be left - Those who believe on the Lord Jesus Christ shall be preserved alive; and not one of these perished in the siege, or afterwards, by those wars.
entries.766a4c4e5c8d7b249f8872d04d759ccc94dcf85e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35781" type="x-p"/> I will bring the third part through the fire - The Christian Church shall endure a great fight of afflictions, by which they shall be refined - not consumed. <div eID="gen35781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35782" type="x-p"/> They shall call on my name - In this way shall they offer all their prayers and supplications to God. <div eID="gen35782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35783" type="x-p"/> I will say, It is my people - The Church that I have chosen in the place of the Jews who have filled up the measure of their iniquity. <div eID="gen35783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35784" type="x-p"/> And they shall say, The Lord is my God - And thus communion shall be established between me and them for ever. Thus there shall be a general restoration.  <chapter eID="Zech.13"/> <div eID="gen35784" type="x-p"/>

entries.de4464798263d4359c47f2dfe3a534ea7e19e0ca: Zec 13:1 <div eID="gen16917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16918" type="x-p"/> The penitential supplication of Israel will lead to a thorough renewal of the nation, since the Lord will open to the penitent the fountain of His grace for the cleansing away of sin and the sanctifying of life. Zec 13:1. <hi type="italic">“In that day will a fountain be opened to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and uncleanness.” </hi> As the Lord Himself pours out the spirit of supplication upon Israel, so does He also provide the means of purification from sin. A fountain is opened, when its stream of water bursts forth from the bosom of the earth (see <reference osisRef="Isa.41.18">Isa 41:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.6">Isa 35:6</reference>). The water, which flows from the fountain opened by the Lord, is a water of sprinkling, with which sin and uncleanness are removed. The figure is taken partly from the water used for the purification of the Levites at their consecration, which is called מי חטּאת, sin-water, or alter of absolution, in Num 8:7, and partly from the sprinkling-water prepared from the sacrificial ashes of the red heifer for purification from the defilement of death, which is called מי נדּה, water of uncleanness, i.e., water which removed uncleanness, in Num 19:9. Just as bodily uncleanness is a figure used to denote spiritual uncleanness, the defilement of sin (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.9">Psa 51:9</reference>), so is earthly sprinkling-water a symbol of the spiritual water by which sin is removed. By this water we have to understand not only grace in general, but the spiritual sprinkling-water, which is prepared through the sacrificial death of Christ, through the blood that He shed for sin, and which is sprinkled upon us for the cleansing away of sin in the gracious water of baptism. The blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth us from all sin (1Jo 1:7; compare 1Jo 5:6).
entries.477023d1dcb47715046f92ebbb21e4ea73b4ca46: Zec 13:2-6 <div eID="gen16918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16919" type="x-p"/> The house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem represent the whole nation here, as in Zec 12:10. This cleansing will be following by a new life in fellowship with God, since the Lord will remove everything that could hinder sanctification. This renewal of life and sanctification is described in Zec 12:2-7. Zec 12:2. <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass in that day, is the saying of Jehovah of hosts, I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, they shall be remembered no more; and the prophets also and the spirit of uncleanness will I remove out of the land.</hi> Zec 12:3. <hi type="italic">And it will come to pass, if a man prophesies any more, his father and his mother, they that begat him, will say to him, Thou must not live, for thou hast spoken deceit in the name of Jehovah: and his father and his mother, they that begat him, will pierce him through because of his prophesying. </hi> Zec 12:4. <hi type="italic">And it will come to pass on that day, the prophets will be ashamed every one of his vision, at his prophesying, and will no more put on a hairy mantle to lie.</hi> Zec 12:5. <hi type="italic">And he will say, I am no prophet, I am a man who cultivates the land; for a man bought me from my youth.</hi> Zec 12:6. <hi type="italic">And if they shall say to him, What scars are these between thy hands? he will say, These were inflicted upon me in the house of my loves.” </hi> The new life in righteousness and holiness before God is depicted in an individualizing form as the extermination of idols and false prophets out of the holy land, because idolatry and false prophecy were the two principal forms in which ungodliness manifested itself in Israel. The allusion to idols and false prophets by no means points to the times before the captivity; for even of gross idolatry, and therefore false prophecy, did not spread any more among the Jews after the captivity, such passages as <reference osisRef="Neh.6.10">Neh 6:10</reference>, where lying prophets rise up, and even priests contract marriages with Canaanitish and other heathen wives, from whom children sprang who could not even speak the Jewish language (Ezr 9:2 ff.; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.23">Neh 13:23</reference>), show very clearly that the danger of falling back into gross idolatry was not a very remote one. Moreover, the more refined idolatry of pharisaic self-righteousness and work-holiness took the place of the grosser idolatry, and the prophets generally depict the future under the forms of the past. The cutting off of the names of the idols denotes utter destruction (cf. Hos 2:19). The prophets are false prophets, who either uttered the thoughts of their hearts as divine inspiration, or stood under the demoniacal influence of the spirit of darkness. This is evident from the fact that they are associated not only with idols, but with the “spirit of uncleanness.” For this, the opposite of the spirit of grace (Zec 12:10), is the evil spirit which culminates in Satan, and works in the false prophets as a lying spirit (1Ki 22:21-23; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.13-Rev.16.14">Rev 16:13-14</reference>). <div eID="gen16919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16920" type="x-p"/> The complete extermination of this unclean spirit is depicted thus in Zec 13:3-6, that not only will Israel no longer tolerate any prophet in the midst of it (Zec 13:3), but even the prophets themselves will be ashamed of their calling (Zec 13:4-6). The first case is to be explained from the law in <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6-Deut.13.11">Deu 13:6-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.18.20">Deu 18:20</reference>, according to which a prophet who leads astray to idolatry, and one who prophesies in his own name or in the name of false gods, are to be put to death. This commandment will be carried out by the parents upon any one who shall prophesy in the future. They will pronounce him worthy of death as speaking lies, and inflict the punishment of death upon him (<hi type="italic">dâqar</hi>, used for putting to death, as in c. Zec 12:10). This case, that a man is regarded as a false prophet and punished in consequence, simply because he prophesies, rests upon the assumption that at that time there will be no more prophets, and that God will not raise them up or send them any more. This assumption agrees both with the promise, that when God concludes a new covenant with His people and forgives their sins, no one will teach another any more to know the Lord, but all, both great and small, will know Him, and all will be taught of God (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.33-Jer.31.34">Jer 31:33-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Isa 54:13</reference>); and also with the teaching of the Scriptures, that the Old Testament prophecy reached to John the Baptist, and attained its completion and its end in Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.13">Mat 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Luk 16:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17">Mat 5:17</reference>). At that time will those who have had to do with false prophecy no longer pretend to be prophets, or assume the appearance of prophets, or put on the hairy garment of the ancient prophets, of Elias for example, but rather give themselves out as farm-servants, and declare that the marks of wound inflicted upon themselves when prophesying in the worship of heathen gods are the scars of wounds which they have received (Zec 13:4-6). בּושׁ מן, to be ashamed on account of (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>), not to desist with shame. The form הנּבאתו in Zec 13:4 instead of הנּבאו (Zec 13:3) may be explained from the fact that the verbs לא and לה frequently borrow forms from one another (Ges. §75, Anm. 20-22). On אדּרת שׂער, see at 2Ki 1:8. למען כּחשׁ, to lie, i.e., to give themselves the appearance of prophets, and thereby to deceive the people. The subject to ואמר in Zec 13:5 is אישׁ from Zec 13:4; and the explanation given by the man is not to be taken as an answer to a question asked by another concerning his circumstances, for it has not been preceded by any question, but as a confession made by his own spontaneous impulse, in which he would repudiate his former calling. The verb הקנה is not a <hi type="italic">denom.</hi> of מקנה, <hi type="italic">servum facere, servo uti </hi>(Maurer, Koehler, and others), for <hi type="italic">miqneh</hi> does not mean slave, but that which has been acquired, or an acquisition. It is a simple <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> of <hi type="italic">qânâh</hi> in the sense of acquiring, or acquiring by purchase, not of selling. That the statement is an untruthful assertion is evident from Zec 13:6, the two clauses of which are to be taken as speech and reply, or question and answer. Some one asks the prophet, who has given himself out as a farm-servant, where the stripes (<hi type="italic">makkōth</hi>, strokes, marks of strokes) between his hands have come from, and he replies that he received them in the house of his lovers. אשׁר הכּיתי, ἅς (sc., πληγάς) ἐπλήγην: cf. Ges. §143, 1. The questioner regards the stripes or wounds as marks of wounds inflicted upon himself, which the person addressed had made when prophesying, as is related of the prophets of Baal in 1Ki 18:28 (see the comm.). The expression “between the hands” can hardly be understood in any other way than as relating to the palms of the hands and their continuation up; the arms, since, according to the testimony of ancient writers (Movers, <hi type="italic">Phöniz</hi>. i. p. 682), in the self-mutilations connected with the Phrygian, Syrian, and Cappadocian forms of worship, the arms were mostly cut with swords or knives. The meaning of the answer given by the person addressed depends upon the view we take of the word מאהבים. As this word is generally applied to paramours, Hengstenberg retains this meaning here, and gives the following explanation of the passage: namely, that the person addressed confesses that he has received the wounds in the temples of the idols, which he had followed with adulterous love, so that he admits his former folly with the deepest shame. But the context appears rather to indicate that this answer is also nothing more than an evasion, and that he simply pretends that the marks were scars left by the chastisements which he received when a boy in the house of either loving parents or some other loving relations.
entries.2f12917eab1fcae389fa005fff4613152b750e3b: Zec 13:7-9 <div eID="gen16920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16921" type="x-p"/> Zec 13:7. <hi type="italic">“Arise, O sword, over my shepherd, and over the man who is my neighbour, is the saying of Jehovah of hosts: smite the shepherd, that the sheep may be scattered; and I will bring back my hand over the little ones.</hi> Zec 13:8. <hi type="italic">And it will come to pass in all the land, is the saying of Jehovah; two parts therein shall be cut off, shall die, and the third remains therein.</hi> Zec 13:9. <hi type="italic">And the third will I bring into the fire, and melt them as silver is melted, and will refine them as gold is refined: it will call upon my name, and I will answer it; I say, It is my people; and it will say, Jehovah my God.”</hi> The summons addressed to the sword, to awake and smite, is a poetical turn to express the thought that the smiting takes place with or according to the will of God. For similar personification of the sword, see Jer 47:6. רעי is the shepherd of Jehovah, since the summons comes from Jehovah. In what sense the person to be smitten is called the shepherd of Jehovah, we may see from the clause על־גּבר עמיתי. The word עמית, which only occurs in the Pentateuch and in Zechariah, who has taken it thence, is only used as a synonym of אח (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.15">Lev 25:15</reference>) in the concrete sense of the nearest one. And this is the meaning which it has in the passage before us, where the construct state expresses the relation of apposition, as for example in אישׁ חסידך (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.8">Deu 33:8</reference>; cf. Ewald, §287, <hi type="italic">e</hi>), the man who is my nearest one. The shepherd of Jehovah, whom Jehovah describes as a man who is His next one (neighbour), cannot of course be a bad shepherd, who is displeasing to Jehovah, and destroys the flock, or the foolish shepherd mentioned in Zec 11:15-17, as Grotius, Umbr., Ebrard, Ewald, Hitzig, and others suppose; for the expression “man who is my nearest one” implies much more than unity or community of vocation, or that he had to feed the flock like Jehovah. No owner of a flock or lord of a flock would call a hired or purchased shepherd his <hi type="italic">‛âmı̄th</hi>. And so God would not apply this epithet to any godly or ungodly man whom He might have appointed shepherd over a nation. The idea of nearest one (or fellow) involves not only similarity in vocation, but community of physical or spiritual descent, according to which he whom God calls His neighbour cannot be a mere man, but can only be one who participates in the divine nature, or is essentially divine. The shepherd of Jehovah, whom the sword is to smite, is therefore no other than the Messiah, who is also identified with Jehovah in Zec 12:10; or the good shepherd, who says of Himself, “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30). The masculine form הך in the summons addressed to the sword, although חרב itself is feminine, may be accounted for from the personification of the sword; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>, where sin (חטּאת, fem.) is personified as a wild beast, and construed as a masculine. The sword is merely introduced as a weapon used for killing, without there being any intention of defining the mode of death more precisely. The smiting of the shepherd is also mentioned here simply for the purpose of depicting the consequences that would follow with regard to the flock. The thought is therefore merely this: Jehovah will scatter Israel or His nation by smiting the shepherd; that is to say, He will give it up to the misery and destruction to which a flock without a shepherd is exposed. We cannot infer from this that the shepherd himself is to blame; nor does the circumstance that the smiting of the shepherd is represented as the execution of a divine command, necessarily imply that the death of the shepherd proceeds directly from God. According to the biblical view, God also works, and does that which is done by man in accordance with His counsel and will, and even that which is effected through the sin of men. Thus in <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa 53:10</reference> the mortal sufferings of the Messiah are described as inflicted upon Him by God, although He had given up His soul to death to bear the sin of the people. In the prophecy before us, the slaying of the shepherd is only referred to so far as it brings a grievous calamity upon Israel; and the fact is passed over, that Israel has brought this calamity upon itself by its ingratitude towards the shepherd (cf. Zec 11:8, Zec 11:12). The flock, which will be dispersed in consequence of the slaying of the shepherd, is the covenant nation, i.e., neither the human race nor the Christian church as such, but the flock which the shepherd in Zec 11:4. had to feed. At the same time, Jehovah will not entirely withdraw His hand from the scattered flock, but “bring it back over the small ones.” The phrase השׁיב יד על, to bring back the hand over a person (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>), i.e., make him the object of his active care once more, is used to express the employment of the hand upon a person either for judgment or salvation. It occurs in the latter sense in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference> in relation to the grace which the Lord will manifest towards Jerusalem, by purifying it from its dross; and it is used here in the same sense, as Zec 13:8, Zec 13:9 clearly show, according to which the dispersion to be inflicted upon Israel will only be the cause of ruin to the greater portion of the nation, whereas it will bring salvation to the remnant.<hi type="italic">Zec 13:8</hi> and Zec 13:9 add the real explanation of the bringing back of the hand over the small ones. צערים (lit., a participle of צער, which only occurs here) is synonymous with צעיר or צעור (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.3">Jer 14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.4">Jer 48:4</reference>, <hi type="italic">chethib</hi>), the small ones in a figurative sense, the miserable ones, those who are called עניּי הצּאן in Zec 11:7. It naturally follows from this, that the צערים are not identical with the whole flock, but simply form a small portion of it, viz., “the poor and righteous in the nation, who suffer injustice” (Hitzig). “The assertion that the flock is to be scattered, but that God will bring back His hand to the small ones, evidently implies that the small ones are included as one portion of the entire flock, for which God will prepare a different fate from that of the larger whole which is about to be dispersed” (Kliefoth). <div eID="gen16921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16922" type="x-p"/> On the fulfilment of this verse, we read in <reference osisRef="Matt.26.31-Matt.26.32">Mat 26:31-32</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mark.14.27">Mar 14:27</reference>, that the bringing back of the hand of the Lord over the small ones was realized first of all in the case of the apostles. After the institution of the Lord’s Supper, Christ told His disciples that that same night they would all be offended because of Him; for it was written, “I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad. But after I am risen again, I will go before you into Galilee.” The quotation is made freely from the original text, the address to the sword being resolved into its actual meaning, “I will smite.” The offending of the disciples took place when Jesus was taken prisoner, and they all fled. This flight was a prelude to the dispersion of the flock at the death of the shepherd. But the Lord soon brought back His hand over the disciples. The promise, “But after my resurrection I will go before you into Galilee,” is a practical exposition of the bringing back of the hand over the small ones, which shows that the expression is to be understood here in a good sense, and that it began to be fulfilled in the whole of the nation of Israel, to which we shall afterwards return. This more general sense of the words is placed beyond the reach of doubt by Zec 13:8 and Zec 13:9; for Zec 13:8 depicts the misery which the dispersion of the flock brings upon Israel, and Zec 13:9 shows how the bringing back of the hand upon the small ones will be realized in the remnant of the nation. The dispersion of the flock will deliver two-thirds of the nation in the whole land to death, so that only one-third will remain alive. כּל־הארץ is not the whole earth, but the whole of the holy land, as in Zec 14:9-10; and הארץ, in Zec 12:12, the land in which the flock, fed by the shepherds of the Lord, i.e., the nation of Israel, dwells. פּי־שׁנים is taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.21.17">Deu 21:17</reference>, as in 2Ki 2:9; it is used there for the double portion inherited by the first-born. That it is used here to signify two-thirds, is evident from the remaining השּׁלישׁית. “The whole of the Jewish nation,” says Hengstenberg, “is introduced here, as an inheritance left by the shepherd who has been put to death, which inheritance is divided into three parts, death claiming the privileges of the first-born, and so receiving two portions, and life one, - a division similar to that which David made in the case of the Moabites (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>).” יגועוּ is added to יכּרתוּ, to define יכּרת more precisely, as signifying not merely a cutting off from the land by transportation (cf. Zec 14:2), but a cutting off from life (Koehler). גּוע, <hi type="italic">exspirare</hi>, is applied both to natural and violent death (for the latter meaning, compare <reference osisRef="Gen.7.21">Gen 7:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.22.20">Jos 22:20</reference>). The remaining third is also to be refined through severe afflictions, to purify it from everything of a sinful nature, and make it into a truly holy nation of God. For the figure of melting and refining, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa 48:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.6">Jer 9:6</reference>; Mal 3:3; Psa 66:10. For the expression in <hi type="italic">Zec 13:9</hi>, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa 65:24</reference>; and for the thought of the whole verse, Zec 8:8, Hos 2:23, <reference osisRef="Jer.24.7">Jer 24:7</reference>; Jer 30:22. The cutting off of the two-thirds of Israel commenced in the Jewish war under Vespasian and Titus, and in the war for the suppression of the rebellion led by the pseudo-Messiah <hi type="italic">Bar Cochba</hi>. It is not to be restricted to these events, however, but was continued in the persecutions of the Jews with fire and sword in the following centuries. The refinement of the remaining third cannot be taken as referring to the sufferings of the Jewish nation during the whole period of its present dispersion, as C. B. Michaelis supposes, nor generally to the tribulations which are necessary in order to enter into the kingdom of God, to the seven conflicts which the true Israel existing in the Christian church has to sustain, first with the two-thirds, and then and more especially with the heathen (Zec 12:1-9, Zec 12:14). For whilst Hengstenberg very properly objects to the view of Michaelis, on the ground that in that case the unbelieving portion of Judaism would be regarded as the legitimate and sole continuation of Israel; it may also be argued, in opposition to the exclusive reference in the third to the Christian church, that it is irreconcilable with the perpetuation of the Jews, and the unanimous entrance of all Israel into the kingdom of Christ, as taught by the Apostle Paul. Both views contain elements of truth, which must be combined, as we shall presently show. <div eID="gen16922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16923" type="x-p"/> All nations will be gathered together by the Lord against Jerusalem, and will take the city and plunder it, and lead away the half of its inhabitants into captivity (Zec 14:1, Zec 14:2). The Lord will then take charge of His people; He will appear upon the Mount of Olives, and by splitting this mountain, prepare a safe way for the rescue of those that remain, and come with all His saints (Zec 14:3-5) to complete His kingdom. From Jerusalem a stream of salvation and blessing will pour over the whole land (Zec 14:6-11); the enemies who have come against Jerusalem will be miraculously smitten, and destroy one another (Zec 14:12-15). The remnant of the nations, however, will turn to the Lord, and come yearly to Jerusalem, to keep the feast of Tabernacles (Zec 14:16-19); and Jerusalem will become thoroughly holy (Zec 14:20, Zec 14:21). From this brief description of the contents, it is perfectly obvious that our chapter contains simply a further expansion of the summary announcement of the judgment upon Israel, and its refinement (Zec 13:7-9). Zec 14:1, Zec 14:2 show how the flock is dispersed, and for the most part perishes; Zec 14:2-5, how the Lord brings back His hand over the small ones; vv. 6-21, how the rescued remnant of the nation is endowed with salvation, and the kingdom of God completed by the reception of the believers out of the heathen nations. There is no essential difference in the fact that the nation of Israel is the object of the prophecy in Zec 13:7-9, and Jerusalem in ch. 14. Jerusalem, as the capital of the kingdom, is the seat of Israel, the nation of God; what happens to it, happens to the people and kingdom of God.  <chapter eID="Zech.13"/> <div eID="gen16923" type="x-p"/>
