Chapter 13
Zechariah 13:1
1. In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness.
1. In die illo erit fons apertus domui Davidis, et incolis Ierosolymae, ad peccatum et ad immunditiam (vel, ad expiationem et aspersionem.)
 
From this verse we again learn, that Zechariah promised the spirit of repentance to the Jews, so that they would find God still propitious to them, when their circumstances were brought to the verge of despair: for it would not have been enough for them to feel sorrow, except God himself became propitious and merciful to them. He had said indeed that the Spirit of grace and of commiserations would be poured forth; but he had not as yet taught clearly what he now adds respecting remission and pardon. After having then declared that there would be felt by the Jews the bitterest sorrow, because they had as it were pierced God, he now mentions the fruit of this repentance. And hence also appears what Paul means by sorrow not to be repented of; for it generates repentance unto salvation. When then our sorrow is blessed by the Lord, the end is to be regarded; for our hearts are thereby raised up to joy. But the issue of repentance, as Zechariah declares here, is ablution: and he alludes to the legal rites when he says,
A fountain shall be opened to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. We know that formerly under the law many washings were prescribed to the Jews; and when any one had become defiled, to wash himself was the remedy. It is certain that water was of no value to cleanse the heart; but the sins of men, we know, are expiated by the death of Christ, so that true ablution is by the blood which he shed for us.
Jerome and Cyril say that the “fountain” is baptism; but Theodoret with more wisdom considered it to be the blood of Christ. Marckius regarded it as the grace of God flowing to us through the merits of the Redeemer, and applied for justification and sanctification. The word “fountain,” says Drusius, intimates the perennity and abundance of grace. — Ed.
Hence the types of the law ought no doubt to be referred to this blood. The meaning is that God would be reconciled to the Jews when they became touched with sincere sorrow, and that reconciliation would be ready for them, for the Lord would cleanse them from every defilement.
He speaks of a fountain opened; and he no doubt intimates here a difference between the law and the gospel. Water was brought daily to the temple; but it was, we know, for private washings. But Zechariah promises here a perpetual stream of cleansing water; as though he had said, “Ablution will be free to all, when God shall again receive his people into favor.” Though remission of sins was formerly offered under the law, yet it is now much more easily obtained by us; not that God grants a license to sin, but that the way in which our filth is cleansed, has become more evident since the coming of Christ. For the fathers under the law were indeed fully assured that God was so propitious as not to impute sins; but where was the pledge of ablution? In the sprinkling of blood, and that blood was the blood of a calf or a lamb. Now since we know that we have been redeemed by Christ, and that our souls are sprinkled with his blood by the hidden power of the Holy Spirit, it is doubtless the same as though God had not only set before our eyes our ablution, but also placed it as it were in our hands, while to the fathers it was more obscure or shown to them at a distance.
And he says, To the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. He had before restricted God’s favor to that city, that he might goad the Jews, who had preferred their outward gratifications to so great a happiness; for they thought themselves happy in their exile, because they inhabited a pleasant and fruitful country, and enjoyed quietness and peace; and thus it happened that they despised the deliverance offered to them. Hence the Prophet promises here to the citizens of Jerusalem and to the royal family a fountain in which they might wash away their filth; for from Sion was the law to go forth, and from Jerusalem the word of the Lord. (Isaiah 2:2.) And we know that from thence were taken the first-fruits of the new Church.
The house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem were specifically mentioned, says Grotius, because they had grievously offended. The design seems to have been to point out those who had been most guilty, who had been themselves the murderers of their own Messiah. This fountain was yet opened for them. — Ed.
What we have before seen respecting God’s favor being extended farther, is no objection; for both events were in their due order fulfilled, as God blessed the tribe of Judah, who trusted in his promises and returned to their own country, and afterwards extended wider his favor, and gathered into one body those who had been dispersed through distant parts of the world.
He adds, For sin and for uncleanness, or as some read, “for sprinkling,” which is by no means suitable, except the word “sin” be taken for expiation. The word is derived from נדד, nedad, but it often means sprinkling, sometimes uncleanness, and sometimes the uncleanness of women, and so some render it here. The verb signifies to remove or to separate; and hence נדה, nede, is the removal of a woman from her husband during her uncleanness, but it is applied to designate any uncleanness. It might indeed be taken here for the uncleanness of women, as an instance of a part for the whole; but I am led by the context to render it uncleanness. Now if we translate חטאת, chathat, sin, then נדה, nede, must be rendered uncleanness; but if the first be expiation, then the second may be sprinkling: and this meaning I am disposed to take, for under the law sins were cleansed by sacrifices as well as by washings.
 
For sin and defilement, Newcome
For guilt and for uncleanness, Henderson
Our version cannot be mended “for sin and for uncleanness.” The latter word, [נדה], has been strangely rendered by some. Its first meaning is removal or separation, which took place in case of uncleanness: but it is also used to designate the cause of removal, even uncleanness, and that generally, as we find from Ezra 9:11, where the “land” is said to be “unclean ([נדה]) with the filthiness ([נדת]) of the people,” or rather polluted with the pollution of the people “of the lands.” It is used in this text as synonymous with [טמא], which means what is unclean, defiled, or polluted. See Ezra 6:21
This verse is most strangely rendered by the Septuagint, in a way quite unaccountable. The three other versions — Aq., Sym., and Theod., — are not very far from the original. — Ed.
The import of the whole then is — that though the Jews had in various ways defiled themselves, so that they were become filthy before God, and their uncleanness was abominable, yet a fountain would be prepared for them, by which they might cleanse themselves, so as to come before God pure and clean. We hence see that it was the Prophet’s object to show, that the repentance of which he had spoken would not be useless, for there would be a sure issue, when God favored the Jews, and showed himself propitious to them, and already pacified, and even provided for them a cleansing by the blood of his only-begotten Son, so that no filth might prevent them to call on him boldly and in confidence; for instead of the legal rites there would be the reality, as their hearts would be sprinkled by the Spirit, so that they would be purified by faith, and would thus cast away all their filth.
Prayer
Grant, Almighty God, that since thou hast been pleased to adopt us as thy people, and from being thine enemies, profane and reprobate, to make us the children of Abraham, that we might be to thee a holy heritage, — O grant, that through the whole course of our life we may so repent as to attain thy mercy, which is daily set before us in thy gospel, and of which thou hast given us a sure pledge in the death of thy only Son, so that we may become more and more humble before thee, and labor to form our life according to the rule of righteousness, and so loathe ourselves, that we may at the same time be allured by the sweetness of thy goodness to call upon thee, and that being thus united to thee, we may be confirmed in the faith, until we shall reach that blessed rest which has been procured for us by the blood of thy Son Jesus Christ. — Amen.
 
Lecture One Hundred and Sixty-third
Zechariah 13:2
2. And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they shall no more be remembered: and also I will cause the prophets and the unclean spirit to pass out of the land.
2. Et erit in die illo, dicit Iehova exercituum, Excidam (vel, delebo) nomina simulachrorum e terra, et non erunt in memoria amplius; atque etiam Prohetas et spiritum immundum auferam (vel, exterminabo, ad verbam est, transire faciam) e terra.

               <ns0:head>CHAP. XIII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 IN that day <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">When the Lamb of God shall be offered up a Sacrifice for mankind, and the Gospel shall be preached in which the glad Tydings of our Redemption are publisht.</ns0:note> there shall be a fountain <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">By water, and Ceremonial washings was legal pollution in many cases purged away, and much of the legal Service stood in divers washings, but all these were Shadows and Types, here is that they typifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed. The matchless healing, and purging Fountain, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Blood of Christ here is the true <ns0:hi>Siloam</ns0:hi> which never fail'd to heal any that rightly used it, 'tis Christ.</ns0:note> open<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Spouse is to Christ a Fountain sealed, but Christ is to sinners a Fountain opened; under the Law he was as the waters of the Temple, for the <ns0:hi>Iew</ns0:hi>; but now he is opened to us <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> free to all, and of easie access, and of Soveraign vertue to heal.</ns0:note> to the house of David, <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">He was every where nearest to them, and though his own Kindred did some of them slight him, and not believe in him, yet some others did, and it may intimate to us the first tender of Grace made to his own, to whom he came, though they received him not; or the Royal Family some of them will be benefitted by it, and all of them need it; no outward priviledge can secure us against poyson of sin, Grace alone, this Fountain only can purge it away in great, and noble; or mean, and base.</ns0:note> and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To all the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> before the <ns0:hi>Gentiles, To you first saith the Apostle, God hath sent his Son,</ns0:hi> but in that 'tis opened, 'tis to us <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> also. <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> as Image of the whole Church, takes in the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> so Inhabitants of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> are all to whom the Gospel is prea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ched, all penit<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>nts.</ns0:note> for sin, and <ns0:note place="margin">

                     </ns0:gap>

Psal. 16.4. Ezek. 30.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>. Hos. 2.17.</ns0:note> cut off the names of the idols out of the land <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Utterly destroy Idols and Idolatry, <ns0:hi>Satan fell from Heaven like Lightning,</ns0:hi> as Christ tells us when the Gospel was preacht by those he sent, and 'tis known the Birth of Christ silenced the Devil, that he could no more give answer to those that enquired at his Oracles, the light of the Gospel is such, that none of the Idols can bear it. The Devil put it into the heads of the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> to keep Christ from being recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved by publick allowance for a God, because he would turn out all the rest of them.</ns0:note>, and they shall no more be remembred <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">With veneration, sacrifices, gifts, erecting of Temples, depending on, or consulting with them; they shall be remembred and abhorred, whereas before they were remembred and ador'd.</ns0:note>: and also I will cause the prophets <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either those that being Priests to Idols, did consult with them, and pretend to foretel future events, or more likely the false Prophets among the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> who are Prophets as Idols are Gods. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Devil which sets the false Prophets on work, Christ cast many out of persons possessed, and by his Doctrine still doth cast out Satan.</ns0:note>, and the unclean spirit <ns0:hi>i</ns0:hi> to pass out of the land <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 12.43. Mar. 1.29.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And it shall come to pass, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> when any shall yet prophesie <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whosoever he be that shall pretend hereafter to prophe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sie through the instigation of that unclean Spirit, for it can be from no other, when the Lord shall have fully revealed his mind to us.</ns0:note>, then his father and his mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther that begat him <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">His dearest friends, they who are by nature nearest to him who begat him.</ns0:note>, shall say unto him <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">Shall discourse him, and inform him what the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> directeth in this case.</ns0:note>, Thou shalt not live <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which I take to be not the sentence condemnatory, for being private persons, they could not condemn him; but it is a repetition of the Law which saith, such shall not live, and then it amounts to this, a false Prophet ought not to live, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13.6, 8. what then dost thou do to break this Law, and endanger thy Life? Thou oughtest to dye for this by the Law; the Father and Mother thus should admonish and shew the matter of Law and danger, but not judicially pass sentence<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and determin what shall be done.</ns0:note>: for thou speakest lies in the Name of the LORD <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Thou fallest under that Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13.6.</ns0:note>: and his father, and his mother that begat him, shall thrust him through <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, wound, chastise with stripes that may leave their marks behind them, or rather shall sharply re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prove him, and with cutting words terrifie him from the like practice: You read of words that are piercing words, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 12.18. words that run through as a Sword, and the <ns0:hi>Chaldee</ns0:hi> Paraphrast on this of our Prophet allows the Father and Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther to deal sharply with their Son, they shall rebuke cuttingly; besides, if 'twere to be understood of killing, the Law directs to stone such a one, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13.10. not to run him through with Lance or Sword.</ns0:note> when he prophesieth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And it shall come to pass <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">By this means it will come to pass, such sharp reproofs, such impartial threats, such convincing arguments will have a good effect.</ns0:note> in that day <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> the prophets shall be ashamed <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">These Prophets will see their Errour, and be ashamed, and give over what they blush at, and is their shame.</ns0:note> every one of his vision: when he hath prophesied; neither shall they wear a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 King.1.8.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>a gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of hair.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> rough garment <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Such Garments the true Prophets were wont to wear, and these cheats had used them for a cover to their jugling Hy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pocrisie; but when throughly convinced, none shall need pull, they will themselves cast off those Garments.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>to lie.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> to deceive <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By first seeming to be more holy and strict than they are; and next on such ill grounded opinion of the holiness of their persons draw them into their Opinions, Religion, and Practice. 'Tis an excellent work of the Grace of God to recover deceivers, and to make them turn off the deceiver, and deal plainly and faithfully with others, and themselves.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 But he shall say, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> no prophet, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> an husbandman: for man taught me to keep cattel from my youth.<ns0:note place="bottom">This verse is this reclaimed man's recantation, or renunciati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of his former course, and his solemn promise to take up his own Calling, and become a plain honest man, and live up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on his Labour, to which he was trained up from his youth, and is sorry he ever left it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> shall say unto him, What <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> these wounds <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This verse continueth the account of the reclaimed Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, and supposeth what is usual that some will enquire what the meaning of the marks or impressions on his hands, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther they were not such as appropriated him to an Idol, or de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clared him a profest Diviner.</ns0:note> in thine hands? Then he shall answer <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">plainly and fully no such as you imagine.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>Those</ns0:hi> with which I was wounded <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> the house of my friends <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">But the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ars of the wounds my stubbornness deserved, and the love of my friends gave me under a severe Discipline, to recover me from ruining my self and others by Impostures, and Lies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

Man my fellow speaks Christ man with us, and God with his Father, God-man in one person.</ns0:note>, saith the LORD of hosts: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Math. 26.31. Mark 14.27.</ns0:note> smite the shepherd <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This great and good shepherd shall be smitten, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> die for my sheep, and before he dieth, shall suffer much for them.</ns0:note>, and the sheep shall be scattered <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">As affrighted, destitute of one to look after them, and which must be partakers in sufferings with their shepherd.</ns0:note> and I will turn mine hand <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">God will, say some, turn his hand against the little ones, smite them too; but, others say, this turning the hand is in favour, and for pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tection, 'tis a hand turned over them, as if he would keep the blow off them, while others fitter to bear it do suffer.</ns0:note> upon the little ones <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">New, and therefore weak Converts and Disciples.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">Many words are spent by Interpreters to shew what they think to be the connexion of the words; it is easier to say what are the contents and design of them. It is possible they are subjoined to the former to vindicate Christ from the suspi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cion of an Impostor, though he was wounded, for this his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther did foretel by <ns0:hi>Zechariah</ns0:hi> 490 years more or less before<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hand, so that these wounds are not marks of an Impostor, but testimonies of his Truth, and that he is the Messiah.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And it shall come to pass, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> in all the land <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Of <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> or the whole World.</ns0:note>, saith the LORD, two parts <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Not precisely two, but more largely the greater part by far.</ns0:note> therein shall be cut off, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> die, but the third <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A Temporal Death, by the Sword of <ns0:hi>Titus,</ns0:hi> or an eternal death under unbelief and rejecting Christ.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> A remnant, the lesser part, yet as many as are chosen.</ns0:note> shall be left therein <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Shall escape or be preserved and saved.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">This <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> may be a prediction of the great slaughter <ns0:hi>Titus</ns0:hi> made among the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and also an Emblem of the multitudes of them that perish, and paucity of them that are saved.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And I will bring the third part through the fire <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That part that is preserved shall be brought into afflicti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons hot as fire.</ns0:note>, and will <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 1.6, 7.</ns0:note> refine them as silver is re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fined <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">These Afflictions shall purifie them, and so better them as Silver and Gold are bettered by the Furnace, made fitter to be Vessels of honour.</ns0:note>, and will try them as gold is tried: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 50.15.</ns0:note> they shall call on my name <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Pray to me and own me for their God.</ns0:note>, and I will hear <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">I will answer them, and own them for my People, my purified People, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> them: I will say, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 144.15.</ns0:note> It <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my people; and they shall say, The LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my God.</ns0:p>
